questions.question: Describe the working and living conditions of enslaved field hands on a cotton plantation and two methods owners used to control them.
questions.expected_answer: Work from before sunrise to after sunset six days a week under the gang system driven by overseers with whips; picking quotas at harvest; children working young. Small, crowded cabins with dirt floors; rations of cornmeal and salted pork; rough clothing. Control: whipping and other violence, the threat of selling family members, passes and patrols, laws forbidding reading, weapons or testimony.

questions.question: Explain how songs, stories and faith helped enslaved people survive and resist.
questions.expected_answer: Work songs with call and response set rhythm and built unity; spirituals such as Go Down, Moses expressed sorrow, faith and longing for freedom, possibly with hidden messages; trickster tales like Brer Rabbit showed the weak outwitting the strong; enslaved people interpreted Christianity as a message of liberation and worshipped secretly in the invisible church. These preserved dignity, identity, hope and African traditions.

questions.question: Give five examples of individual or everyday resistance to slavery.
questions.expected_answer: Working slowly or pretending to be ill; breaking tools or damaging crops; taking food; learning to read and write in secret (e.g. Frederick Douglass); running away temporarily or permanently; forming maroon communities; buying freedom; keeping names, culture and family alive; violence against owners.
